title: Ancient Rome · Episode 1
chapters: Hannibal: the general who crossed the Alps
Julius Caesar and the end of the Republic

units.t: Ancient Rome. Episode one.
In this episode: The Roman Republic, Hannibal: the general who crossed the Alps, Julius Caesar and the end of the Republic and Cleopatra: the last pharaoh.
Part one. The Roman Republic.
For nearly 500 years Rome had no king.
Its system of checks and balances inspired the founders of modern republics.
No more kings.
According to Roman tradition, Rome was founded in 753 BC and ruled by seven kings.
The last, Tarquin the Proud, was overthrown in about 509 BC after his son assaulted a noblewoman, Lucretia.
How much is legend is debated, but Romans came to hate the idea of a king, or rex.
They created a res publica, 'the people's affair', the origin of our word republic.
Instead of a king, Rome elected two consuls each year.
They commanded armies and led government, but each could veto the other, and after a year they stepped down and could be prosecuted for abuses.
The Senate, mostly former officials sitting for life, controlled public money and foreign affairs.
In a real emergency, a dictator could be appointed, but only for six months.
Votes and ranks.
Adult male citizens voted in assemblies, but votes were counted by group.
In the assembly that elected consuls, groups were arranged by wealth and the richest voted first, so the result was often settled before poorer citizens were asked.
Ambitious men climbed a ladder of offices, the cursus honorum, from quaestor to praetor to consul.
Campaigning was costly, so a career needed money, famous ancestors or powerful friends.
Early Rome was dominated by patricians, a few old families.
Everyone else was a plebeian.
In the Conflict of the Orders, plebeians repeatedly walked out together, a kind of general strike.
They won officials called tribunes, who could veto harmful actions, and the Twelve Tables, about 450 BC, which put the laws on public display.
In 367 BC they won the right to become consul.
Conquest abroad.
Rome gradually took over Italy, often making defeated peoples allies who kept local self-government but supplied soldiers.
That gave it huge reserves of manpower.
Then it clashed with Carthage, a wealthy trading city in modern Tunisia.
In three Punic Wars between 264 and 146 BC, Rome built its first serious navy and eventually won.
The most famous moment came in 218 BC, when the Carthaginian general Hannibal marched an army, with war elephants, over the Alps into Italy.
At Cannae in 216 BC he destroyed a much larger Roman army.
But Rome refused to negotiate and fought on.
In 146 BC it destroyed Carthage completely, the same year it sacked Corinth in Greece.
Cracks in the system.
Conquest brought enormous wealth, but mostly to the rich, who bought up land and built large estates worked by enslaved captives.
Small farmers, away fighting for years, lost their farms and drifted to Rome.
The brothers Tiberius and Gaius Gracchus tried to give public land to the poor and were killed in 133 and 121 BC, a shocking break with custom.
Around 107 BC the general Marius is traditionally credited with opening the army to poor volunteers.
These soldiers depended on their commanders for pay and for land when they retired.
Their loyalty shifted from the Republic to the generals who led them.
Strongmen and legacy.
In 88 BC the general Sulla marched his army on Rome itself, later becoming dictator with no six-month limit.
Pompey, Crassus and Julius Caesar then competed for power.
Caesar's dictatorship ended with his assassination in 44 BC.
His heir Octavian became sole ruler and took the name Augustus in 27 BC.
The institutions survived on paper, but real power sat with one man.
The Republic's ideas lived on.
The founders of the United States studied Rome closely, creating a Senate, dividing power between branches and writing as 'Publius'.
Australia's Senate has a Roman name, though its design owes more to the American model.
Fixed terms, vetoes, published laws and legal process all have Roman roots, as does 'candidate', from the Latin for 'dressed in white'.
The key idea: Rome expelled its last king around 509 BC and built a republic where power was shared, short-term and checked.
Part two. Hannibal: the general who crossed the Alps.
He marched elephants over the Alps and destroyed Roman armies one after another.
So why did Rome, not Hannibal, win the war?
Rome, Carthage and revenge.
In the third century BC, Rome, a rising land power that controlled most of Italy, faced Carthage, a wealthy trading city founded by Phoenicians in what is now Tunisia.
The Romans called Carthaginians Poeni, hence the Punic Wars.
In the first, from 264 to 241 BC, Rome, which had little naval experience, built fleets almost from scratch and won.
Carthage lost Sicily and paid a huge indemnity.
Hamilcar Barca then conquered territory in Spain.
His son Hannibal grew up in military camps there.
Ancient historians tell how the nine-year-old swore at an altar never to be a friend of Rome.
He took command at about twenty-six in 221 BC, and in 218 BC the Second Punic War began.
Over the mountains.
Rome controlled the sea, so Hannibal attacked overland, which no one expected.
In 218 BC he led his army from Spain across the Pyrenees, through southern Gaul and over the Rhône, with war elephants ferried on rafts.
Late in the year, he crossed the Alps.
The journey took about fifteen days in the mountains, through snow, landslides and ambushes by local tribes.

Polybius, who wrote within living memory and claimed to have walked the route, says Hannibal reached Italy with about twenty thousand infantry and six thousand cavalry, a fraction of the force that had left Spain.
Most of the elephants died soon after.
Which pass he used is still debated.
Cannae: the perfect trap.
Hannibal defeated the Romans at the Trebia in 218 BC, then ambushed an army in fog beside Lake Trasimene in 217.
Rome responded under Quintus Fabius Maximus, who avoided pitched battle and shadowed Hannibal, earning the nickname Cunctator, the delayer.
Frustrated Romans abandoned that approach.
In 216 BC at Cannae, a huge Roman army attacked.
Hannibal placed his weakest troops in the centre, which bent backwards under pressure as planned, drawing the Romans in.
His heavy infantry then closed in from both sides while his cavalry struck from behind.
The Romans were surrounded and slaughtered.
Ancient sources give fifty thousand or more dead, and military academies still study the battle.
Why Rome didn’t fall.
After Cannae, many expected Rome to surrender.
It did not.
The Senate refused to discuss peace, raised new legions, and returned to Fabius’s careful strategy.
Hannibal hoped Rome’s Italian allies would desert in large numbers.
Some, including Capua, did, but most of central Italy stayed loyal and kept supplying men and money.
Hannibal lacked siege equipment and reinforcements to attack Rome, and Carthage sent him little help.
He stayed in Italy about fifteen years, undefeated in major battle yet unable to finish the war.
Meanwhile a brilliant young Roman general, Publius Cornelius Scipio, conquered Carthaginian Spain and invaded North Africa, forcing Carthage to recall Hannibal to defend his home city.
Zama, exile and a myth.
In 202 BC, Scipio and Hannibal met at Zama in North Africa.
Scipio had learnt from his enemy, opening lanes in his lines for Hannibal’s charging elephants to pass through harmlessly, and his cavalry won the day.
Carthage surrendered, gave up its fleet and overseas empire, and paid heavy tribute.
Scipio was honoured with the name Africanus.
Hannibal led Carthage’s government for a time, then fled into exile in the East, and around 183 BC took poison rather than be handed to the Romans.
In the Third Punic War, Rome besieged and destroyed Carthage in 146 BC.
The popular story that the Romans sowed the ground with salt, however, appears to be a modern invention.
The key idea: Carthage’s Barca family wanted revenge after Rome won the First Punic War, and Hannibal inherited that aim.
Part three. Julius Caesar and the end of the Republic.
A brilliant general, a gifted writer, a reckless gambler.
Caesar's rise and murder turned Rome from republic into empire.
Debt and alliances.
Gaius Julius Caesar was born around 100 BC into an old but not wealthy family.
He was charismatic and ambitious, deep in debt from spending on public games and, said his enemies, bribes.
Captured by pirates as a young man, he reportedly joked he would crucify them and, once ransomed, did.
In 63 BC he was elected pontifex maximus, the chief priest, in his thirties.
Even his rival Cicero praised his speaking.
In 60 BC Caesar formed a private alliance with Crassus, Rome's richest man, and Pompey, its most famous general, later called the First Triumvirate.
It was a deal, not an office.
As consul in 59 BC he forced through laws, then secured a five-year command in Gaul, giving him an army of his own.
Gaul and propaganda.
From 58 to 50 BC Caesar conquered all of Gaul, roughly modern France and Belgium.
He bridged the Rhine and crossed to Britain twice.
His greatest victory was Alesia in 52 BC, where he trapped Vercingetorix inside a ring of walls, with another facing outward against a huge relief army.
Ancient writers claimed around a million Gauls died and another million were enslaved.
Historians treat the figures cautiously, but the toll was enormous.
Caesar also wrote about it.
His Commentaries on the Gallic War use plain Latin and call him 'Caesar', so they read like neutral reports.
They were not.
Circulating in Rome, they kept his name in the news and made every war look necessary.
Rubicon and Egypt.
By 50 BC Crassus was dead and Pompey's bond with Caesar had weakened.
The Senate ordered Caesar to give up his army and return as a private citizen, when he would likely face prosecution.
Governors were banned from leading armies into Italy.
In January 49 BC he led a legion across the Rubicon, reportedly saying 'The die is cast.'
Today 'crossing the Rubicon' means passing a point of no return.
In 48 BC he defeated Pompey at Pharsalus.
Pompey fled to Egypt, where he was murdered.
Caesar backed Cleopatra in her struggle with her brother Ptolemy XIII, and she took the throne.
In 47 BC he beat King Pharnaces so quickly he wrote, 'Veni, vidi, vici': I came, I saw, I conquered.
Reformer and dictator.
After further wins in Africa and Spain, Caesar pardoned many former enemies.
This won admiration but left opponents alive and resentful.
He gave land to veterans, founded colonies, extended citizenship and enlarged the Senate.
He also replaced Rome's drifting calendar with a 365-day year and a leap day every four years, the Julian calendar, the basis of ours.
July is named after him.
But in early 44 BC he was named dictator for life, sat on a golden chair and put his portrait on coins, a first for a living Roman.
To many senators, he looked like a king.
The Ides of March.
On 15 March 44 BC, senators led by Marcus Brutus and Gaius Cassius stabbed Caesar to death at a Senate meeting, claiming to save the Republic.
More than 60 men were said to be in the plot, and he suffered 23 wounds.
Instead of restoring the old order, the murder triggered more civil wars.
Caesar's adopted heir Octavian joined Mark Antony to defeat the assassins at Philippi in 42 BC, then beat Antony and Cleopatra at Actium in 31 BC.
In 27 BC the Senate gave Octavian the title Augustus.
He never called himself king, but he was Rome's first emperor, and the Republic was over.
The key idea: Caesar rose through debt, charm and a private deal with Pompey and Crassus, which won him an army.
Part four. Cleopatra: the last pharaoh.
She has been painted as a seductress for two thousand years, mostly by her enemies.
The real Cleopatra was a scholar-queen fighting to keep her country alive.
A Greek queen of Egypt.
Cleopatra VII was born in 69 BC, but her family story begins with Alexander the Great.
After Alexander died, one of his generals, Ptolemy, took control of Egypt and founded a dynasty.
For nearly three hundred years the Ptolemies ruled from Alexandria, the glittering Greek city on the Mediterranean coast.
They presented themselves to Egyptians as pharaohs, but they spoke Greek and often married their own siblings to keep power in the family.
Here is a perspective worth sitting with: Cleopatra lived closer in time to the Moon landing than to the building of the Great Pyramid of Giza.
To her, the pyramids were already ancient monuments, more than two thousand years old.
Brains before beauty.
Hollywood made Cleopatra a famous beauty, but the ancient evidence points elsewhere.
The Greek writer Plutarch, who drew on earlier sources, said her beauty was not in itself incomparable, but her presence was captivating, her conversation charming and her voice delightful.
He reported that she spoke many languages and could talk to foreign envoys without interpreters.
According to Plutarch, she was the first of her dynasty to bother learning Egyptian, the language of the people she ruled.
Her coins show a strong hooked nose and a firm chin, though coin portraits were also political images.
Educated in Alexandria, one of the great centres of learning in the ancient world, she ruled as a skilled, calculating politician.
Caesar and the rolled-up queen.
Cleopatra came to power around 51 BC as co-ruler with her younger brother, Ptolemy XIII, but his advisers soon drove her out.
She raised an army, and the siblings were at war when Julius Caesar arrived in Alexandria in 48 BC, chasing his Roman rival Pompey.
Cleopatra needed to reach Caesar without being caught by her brother’s men.
Plutarch says she was smuggled into the palace by boat at dusk, hidden inside a bag for bedding, the origin of the later legend about a carpet.
Caesar took her side.
After months of fighting in the city, Ptolemy XIII drowned while fleeing, and Cleopatra was restored to the throne.
She later bore a son, Ptolemy Caesar, nicknamed Caesarion.
Antony and Actium.
Cleopatra was in Rome when Caesar was assassinated in 44 BC, and she quickly returned to Egypt.
Mark Antony now controlled Rome’s eastern provinces.
In 41 BC he summoned her to Tarsus, in modern Turkey.
Plutarch describes her arriving on a barge with a gilded stern, purple sails and silver oars, dressed as the goddess Aphrodite.
Whatever the exact details, it was political theatre, and it worked.
They became partners in power and in private, and she had three children with him.
In 34 BC, Antony handed territories to Cleopatra and her children, and his rival Octavian used this as proof that Antony had betrayed Rome to a foreign queen.
At the naval Battle of Actium in 31 BC, their fleet was beaten.
Written by the winners.
A year after Actium, Octavian’s armies closed in on Alexandria.
Antony, believing Cleopatra was already dead, stabbed himself.
Cleopatra died in August 30 BC, aged thirty-nine, rather than be paraded through Rome as a captive.
The famous story says an asp, smuggled to her in a basket of figs, bit her.
Yet even Plutarch admitted nobody knew the truth, and some historians think poison is more likely.
Caesarion was later killed on Octavian’s orders.
Egypt became a Roman province, ending three thousand years of pharaohs.
Because Octavian won, his version dominated, and Roman poets painted Cleopatra as a drunken, power-hungry foreigner.
Historians today see a ruler who used money, diplomacy and alliances to keep Egypt independent.
Her tomb has never been found.
The key idea: Cleopatra belonged to a Greek-speaking dynasty founded by one of Alexander the Great’s generals.
Quick recall. Answer out loud, or just in your head.
Question one. Why did Rome limit each consul to one year and give each a veto over the other?
Answer. So that no man could rule like a king.
Question two. Why did the Barca family want another war with Rome?
Answer. Carthage lost Sicily and paid a huge indemnity.
Question three. What was the First Triumvirate?
Answer. A private pact of Caesar, Pompey and Crassus.
Question four. What was the background of the dynasty Cleopatra belonged to?
Answer. Greek rulers descended from Alexander’s general.
That's the end of this episode. The questions are waiting in your review, so you can lock in what you heard.
